sentences.text: They saved the last place for the last day.
Chapultepec park.
A big tree by a little pond.
That was the last note on the map.
I first read Rulfo here.
Rulfo, Abuelo had explained, was a Mexican writer, and the book — a small strange book of stories called El Llano en Llamas — had been Frida's mother's favorite book for her entire life.
She had a battered copy of it on the shelf in Los Angeles.
Frida had brought it with her.
It was in her bag now.
The park was huge and it took them a while to find the right tree.
But Abuelo knew which one.
It was an enormous ahuehuete — a Mexican bald cypress — probably four hundred years old.
Its trunk was as wide as a small house.
It stood right at the edge of a small pond where ducks were swimming, and there was a low wall of stone around its base where a person could sit.
Abuelo said, "There.
That was her place.
She would sit right there with her back against the trunk.
Not on the wall.
On the ground.
She said the wall was for tourists."
So Frida sat on the ground with her back against the trunk.
Abuelo sat on the wall a little way off, so as not to hover.
Frida opened her mother's copy of the book.
It fell open naturally to a page that had been read many times — the first page of a story called Nos han dado la tierra.
She read a little bit.
She did not understand all the Spanish, though her Spanish was pretty good.
She kept reading.
She read for maybe twenty minutes.
Then she closed the book and she just sat with her back against the tree.
She thought about her mother sitting in this exact spot when she was, maybe, fourteen.
Reading this exact book for the first time.
She thought about her mother's back against this same bark.
She thought about how her mother had loved this place enough to draw a small star for it on her map, thirty years ago.

She thought about how her mother was gone but the tree was here, and would still be here in a hundred years, and would probably still be here in three hundred years, long after Frida herself was gone too.
And this thought did not make her sad.
Or it made her sad in a different way than she was used to.
A softer way.
A larger way.
After a while she got up.
She went to Abuelo.
She sat down beside him on the wall.
She said, "Abuelo.
Can we do something.
Can we — pretend she is here." Abuelo looked at her.
He nodded slowly.
He said, "Yes.
Yes, mi vida.
What did you have in mind." Frida said, "You said at each place you would tell me what you remember of her being there.
And you did.
That is why we came.
But this is the last place.
And I want us to do the last one different.
I want us to tell her — the tree — about her." Abuelo did not understand at first.
Then he did.
"I want us to tell the tree things she would have wanted to know.
If she were here.
About us.
About things that happened after." Abuelo swallowed.
He nodded.
He put his arm around her.
He said, "You start, mi vida." And Frida started.
She talked to the tree, softly, in English mostly with some Spanish, for maybe half an hour.
She told the tree — she told her mother — everything she thought her mother would want to know.
That her father was doing all right, some days.
That Pancho the cat had grown fat.
That Frida had learned to play a little bit of the piano.
That she had made two new friends at school.

That her father sometimes played her mother's records at dinner, and that this was a thing that used to make Frida cry, and that now it made her happy in a strange mixed way, and that she was proud of herself for that.
Then Abuelo talked.
He talked to the tree — to Frida's mother — in Spanish.
Frida did not understand every word.
But she understood some.
He said things about growing older.
About the house being too quiet.
About what he was proud of.
He cried a little.
Frida had not seen him cry before.
She held his hand.
When he was done, he said, "That's enough for today, I think." And they got up and they walked out of the park, and Frida looked back once at the tree, and she thought — I will come back.
I do not know when.
But I will come back.
Frida flew home the next morning.
At the airport Abuelo held her by the shoulders and looked at her for a moment before he let her go.
He said, "Come back next December.
And every December.
I will take you to new places.
Ones your Mamá did not have on her map.
But places she would have wanted to show you.
Yes." "Yes," said Frida.
She hugged him one more time.
And she went through security and she waved from the other side, and Abuelo waved back until she was out of sight.
On the plane home, she looked at the folded map for a long time.
Then she took out a pen — she had brought one on purpose — and she drew, on the back of the map, a new small star.
Not on the printed map her mother had drawn, but on the blank white back of it.
Underneath the star she wrote: The tree at Chapultepec, where I told her about the last two years.
She looked at the small star for a while, then folded the map back up and put it in her pocket.
She thought, next December, I will add another one.
And she felt, for the first time since her mother had died, that she was making a map of her own.
